newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Anti-government student protests spread in Albania.
newsitem.headline: Anti-government student protests spread in Albania.

text.p: Albanian police on Friday used force to stop school pupils joining an anti-government student protest in Tirana but students in Gjirokaster in the south scored a minor win after police said their protest was legal.
Reporters saw plain-clothes police officers slapping and kicking pupils aged between 16 and 18 as they walked towards Tirana university to join a student protest.
"Special forces...were kicking and punching us," said Edvin, aged 16. "I said 'What are you doing? We are your sons, we are the sons of this country'."
Opposition parties charged that President Sali Berisha's ruling right-wing Democratic Party was using armed civilians to rough up protesters.
Rudina, 20, said: "They have punched us and treated us in a very bad way, but we are ready to protest to the end."

The London-based human rights organisation Amnesty International said it had already communicated its concerns to the Albanian authorities over recent police violence during two months of protests and would do so again.

"Police beatings and kicking clearly amounts to ill treatment if there was no violence," Amnesty's Melanie Anderson said. "It seems to me that, regardless of age, this is incorrect behaviour on behalf of the police."
Police prevented Tirana students from beginning a hunger strike on Thursday. Two student leaders who were bundled into cars and reportedly beaten were released on Friday.

Albania has been hit by a wave of demonstrations and violent clashes since January when hundreds and thousands of investors learnt they had lost most of their savings in fraudulent pyramid investment schemes.

While street clashes have abated, students and pupils across the Balkan state have taken up the flame of protest to call for the resignation of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi's government for failing to control the investment schemes.

Dissident deputies within the ruling Democrats have also called on the government to quit but Berisha was likely to face no trouble winning a second term of office in a parliamentary vote next Monday.
There were also signs of discord among employees of Albania's state-run television, who criticised the station's reporting of the unrest and complained of censorship.
Albania's soccer federation said it had postponed all matches indefinitely until the interior ministry and police chiefs around the country could guarantee security.
In Gjirokaster, 230 km (145 miles) south of Tirana, students occupying a university building and on hunger strike appeared to score a minor victory when police acknowledged their action was legal.
Factory workers, town residents and high school pupils gathered around the university in solidarity with the students but police positioned around the building did not intervene.

The Forum for Democracy, grouping 11 opposition parties, including the main Socialist Party, said Tirana police authorities had given them permission to hold a rally at a soccer field on Saturday at 2 p.m. (1300 GMT) but not in the main Skanderbeg Square as requested.
The Forum condemned the police action against students:
"The party in power is responding to the increasing protests with uncontrolled violence for which it has mobilised bands of armed civilians as public forces seem not be enough."
